A memo is a short, official written message used to communicate information within an organization — a company, a government office, a school, or any institution. People inside that organization write memos to other people inside the same organization.

The key word here is within. A memo is an internal document. It is not meant for customers, the public, or anyone outside. The moment a written message goes outside the organization, it becomes a letter or a report — not a memo.
What is a memo for?

People write memos for many reasons:

  • To announce something — a new policy, a change in work hours, an upcoming event
  • To instruct — telling employees what to do or how to do it
  • To document a decision — putting something in writing so it becomes an official record
  • To request something — approval, resources, or action from someone
  • To remind — following up on something that was already discussed verbally

The unifying thread is this: a memo makes something official. When information is in a memo, it is no longer just a casual remark or a conversation that might be forgotten. It is documented, formal, and on the record.
What does a memo look like?

A memo follows a specific, recognizable format. It almost always begins with a standard header that looks like this:

TO: [who it is addressed to]
FROM: [who wrote it]
DATE: [when it was written]
SUBJECT: [what it is about — one line]

After the header comes the body: the actual message. The body is usually short and direct. Memos do not have greetings like "Dear Sir" and do not end with closings like "Yours sincerely." They get straight to the point.
Who writes memos?

Anyone inside an organization can write a memo — a manager to their team, an employee to their manager, one department to another department, or an executive to the entire company. There is no rule that only high-ranking people write memos. What matters is the purpose, not the seniority of the writer.
Memo vs. Email

In today's world, emails have largely replaced paper memos. An email sent inside a company to share a policy update or give instructions is a digital memo. Many people even write their internal emails in memo style — with a clear subject line and a direct, structured body.

So when someone says "send me a memo," they might literally mean a formatted document, or they might simply mean a clear, official, written message on the matter.
Memo vs. Letter

These two are often confused. The difference is simple:

  • A letter goes outside the organization — to a client, a government body, a partner.
  • A memo stays inside the organization.

Letters also have greetings and formal closings; memos do not.
Memo vs. Note
A note is casual and personal — a quick scribble to a friend or colleague. A memo is formal and official. Notes are not usually filed or archived; memos often are, because they serve as records.
One deeper thing to understand

A memo carries weight. When something is communicated in a memo, it signals: this is serious, this is real, pay attention. A boss who verbally tells a team "we are changing the leave policy" is easy to misremember or misquote. A boss who sends a memo about the same thing has created a clear, undeniable record. This is why in professional and legal contexts, important decisions are always "put in a memo" — to make them official and traceable.
In everyday informal usage

Outside of formal workplaces, people also use "memo" loosely in speech. You might hear phrases like:

  • "Somebody forgot to send me the memo" — meaning: someone forgot to inform me about this.
  • "Did you get the memo?" — meaning: did you hear about this new change or decision?

These are informal, often humorous expressions, but they reflect the word's core meaning: a memo is something that carries important information that everyone should know.
Summary in one sentence
A memo is a short, formal, written message sent within an organization to inform, instruct, request, or document something — making it official and on the record.
